title: Generalized causality constraint based on duality symmetry reveals untapped potential of sound absorption

paper_content.abstract: Causality constraints are known to bind sound absorption to a limit that can only be achieved by optimizing the system bandwidth for a specific material thickness. This limit is defined on the assumption of a one-port system, generally causing duality symmetry to be overlooked. Here, we define a generalized causality constraint of sound absorption by investigating reflection and transmission of a two-port hybrid monopole-dipole resonator. With our theory, we show that the absorption limit is approached by relying on the well-established critical coupling as well as by matching effective compressibility and density. We experimentally show that the designed resonator absorbance follows the duality symmetry condition embodied in the large bandwidth reported, confirming an intrinsic connection between duality symmetry and scattering causality. A comparison with a traditional foam liner and other competitive works further validates our findings. Our results reveal previously untapped absorption potential in broadband acoustic metamaterials.
paper_content.introduction:
Causality, a fundamental principle underpinning the asymmetry of unidirectional time flow, governs the upper bound of absorption integral in passive, linear, and time-invariant materials1,2. Former investigations have revealed that achieving perfect absorption at discretized frequencies requires critically coupled non-Hermitian resonances at exceptional points3,4. The manipulation of zeros and poles on the complex plane of the scattering coefficients follows the balance between the mode density and quality factors of the integrated resonator units, thus achieving broadband impedance matching and high absorption. Subsequent key developments have neared this absorption bound, demonstrated by the broadband absorption observed in multiple resonance-based metamaterials across acoustic5, elastic6 and electromagnetic domains7. Studying the absorption bound of causality constraint will guide the design wave functional devices8–11 with optimal broadband performance in the laboratory and pave the way for large-scale industrial applications12.

However, current methodologies neglect a critical question: how do fundamental symmetries dictate absorption bound throughout the entire spectrum? We find clues by considering causality constraints together with duality symmetry13, a fundamental principle embedded in numerous physics equations. For example, the supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory reveals that the strong coupling limit is remarkably equivalent to its weak coupling counterpart, with an interchange of roles between electric and magnetic charges as delineated by Montonen–Olive duality14,15. Maxwell equations are also invariant when swapping the electric and magnetic fields16. Also, duality symmetry is related to the conservation of the helicity of electromagnetic waves, attributed to the invariant degeneracy of permittivity and permeability across different geometries. In acoustics, the implications of duality symmetry are unclear for this context, due to the longitudinal wave nature, which intrinsically prohibits the helicity17. Although the analogy of acoustic duality symmetry has been proposed and investigated in the seminal work17 on the subject, the relationship between acoustic duality and scattering causality–specifically, its impact on the broadband absorption bandwidth bound of two-port systems—remains unexplored.
paper_content.results:
A generalized causality constraint for a two-port absorber
According to refs. 2, 5, 31 the original causality constraint for a one-port acoustic absorber is expressed as follows:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{m}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D}{c_{0} K_{eff}(0)}, (1)

where D represents the sample thickness, c0, K0 are the sound speed and bulk modulus of the background medium (e.g., air or water), and Keff(0) denotes the static effective compressibility (the inverse of the normalized bulk modulus). The variable of integration, d\omega/\omega^{2}, is proportional to d\lambda where \lambda denotes the wavelength. According to energy conservation, the absorption A(\omega) is defined as 1-|Sm(\omega)|2 where Sm(\omega) is the reflection coefficient. The derivation of Eq. (1) assumes a Neumann backing condition, which implies either \partial x p=0 or v=0, corresponding to the scattering process depicted in the left plane of Fig. 1a. Due to mirror symmetry (or anti-symmetry), this boundary condition allows for mapping the pressure field p (or velocity field v) from the left plane to the right plane. Consequently, Eq. (1) is applicable to acoustic problems involving symmetrical pressure excitation and Sm(\omega) becomes the amplitude of monopole scattering, also referred as symmetrical coherent perfect absorption32. How to reduce Keff(0) to relax the stringent constraint? This has attracted great research interests with substantial advances in recent publications9,33–35.

The 1D acoustic equations for harmonic waves can be expressed in a matrix form as: \partial x [p; v] = i\omega [0, \rho; K^{-1}, 0] [p; v], where \rho and K represent the local mass density and bulk modulus, respectively. In this context, we introduce a duality transformation that mixes the pressure and velocity fields:

[p_{\theta}; v_{\theta}] = D(\theta) [p; v] = [\cos\theta, iZ_{0}\sin\theta; i\sin\theta/Z_{0}, \cos\theta] [p; v],

where Z0 = \sqrt{\rho_{0} K_{0}} (see the detailed derivation on acoustic duality transformation with arbitrary \theta in Supplementary Note 1). If we apply a duality transformation with \theta=\pi/2, we specifically consider the exchange p \to v, \rho \to K, and \rho^{-1} \to K^{-1} between Fig. 1a, b. Consequently, the specific impedance Z=p/v is transformed into specific admittance Y=Z^{-1}=v/p. Moreover, in Eq. (1), Sm = (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0), which can be transformed into Sm \to -Sd because (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) \to -(Y-Y0)/(Y+Y0) = -(Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) = -Sm. Also, the backing condition (\partial x p=0) in Fig. 1a is also replaced by the Dirichlet one (p=0) in Fig. 1b. Therefore, the causality constraint for monopole scattering becomes the complimentary version for dipole scattering22:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{d}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D \rho_{eff}(0)}{c_{0} \rho_{0}}, (2)

where Sd(\omega) is the dipole scattering coefficient. In particular, in this case, one can afford near unity absorption over a reasonably large frequency range for a thin absorber, owing to the generally large ratio of \rho_{eff}(0)/\rho_{0}, i.e., the large imaginary part of \rho_{eff}(\omega) around the dynamic absorbing frequency leads to large static and real-valued \rho_{eff}(0), allowed by Kramer–Kronig relations.

According to the energy conservation and Eq. (3), 1-A(\omega) = |R(\omega)|2+|T(\omega)|2 = 1/2(|Sm(\omega)|2+|Sd(\omega)|2) \geq |Sm(\omega)||Sd(\omega)|. The last relation is derived from the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, or more briefly the AM–GM inequality. By converting this into the causality constraint, we have:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln(1-A(\omega)) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \ln \left| S_{m}(\omega) \right|^{2} + \ln \left| S_{d}(\omega) \right|^{2} \right) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{\pi}{c_{0} L} \left( \frac{1}{K_{eff}(0)} + \frac{\rho_{eff}(0)}{\rho_{0}} \right) = \Gamma, (4)

where L=2D (the defined thickness is effectively doubled due to mirror symmetric boundaries) and \Gamma is the established bound for the two-port setup, reflecting the static material properties. Optimal broadband absorption is defined by the proposed two-port causality constraint. Importantly, the fundamental principle lies on the fact that at long wavelength limit, all 3D scatterings of two-port problems are dominated by long wavelength scatterings as per the weighting factor (1/\omega^{2}). So, the mathematical form of causality constraint inherently embeds the role of duality for two-port 1D systems.
paper_content.methods:
The simulation was carried out using the COMSOL Multiphysics commercial software, specifically employing the FEM facilitated through the “pressure acoustics, frequency domain” module. The simulation setup included monitoring of incident and transmitted waves via two ports located at the boundaries of the model. The lossy components of the CHR structures, specifically the resonators’ necks and the coupling neck between cavities, were calculated by using the narrow region model. In cases where the cavities were filled with a highly absorptive porous foam69, the Johnson–Champoux–Allard model was utilized, characterized by the following parameters (also adopted from ref. 69): porosity \phi=0.94, fluid resistance Rf=32000 [Pa·s/m2], tortuosity factor \alpha=1.06, viscous characteristic length Lv=56 [\mu m], thermal characteristic length Lth=110 [\mu m]. These parameters were consistently applied across different simulations (including the foam liner in Fig. 5) to maintain a benchmark for comparison. For simulations in the time domain, the “pressure acoustics, time explicit” interface was employed.

The geometrical specifications of the single CHR are as follows (see the marked dimensions in Supplementary Fig. 2): diameter D=1.5cm, length L=2.5cm, l=0.4L, coupling channel diameter d=0.625mm, width w=1.5mm, thickness t=0.95mm, cavity height H=6.25mm, radius R=10.67mm, \tau1=3mm, \tau2=2mm. The perforated rate (or ventilation ratio) \phi=S/S0 = (\pi H^{2})/(\pi D^{2})=0.25, where S represents the cross-sectional area at the narrowest part of the main duct, and S0 denotes the wave-front area or duct cross-sectional area. The thickness of other partition walls is standardized at \Delta w=1mm. A 1/32 reduced model features a sector angle of 360/32=11.25.

The scaling of the sample in Fig. 5 adheres to the following rules: Vc \to \alpha Vc, L \to \alpha^{1/2} L, \phi \to \alpha^{-1/2} \phi, where \alpha is the scaling factor and Vc is the cavity volume occupied by porous foam. The total thickness of the integrated sample is calculated as L = (\sqrt{0.5} + \sqrt{1.5} + \sqrt{2.5} + \sqrt{4}) L0 + 3\Delta w = 14.1cm.

For the acoustic-flow interaction simulations (see Supplementary Fig. 8), the flow resistance was calculated using the “linearized Navier-Stokes, frequency domain” interface. The background pressure drop \Delta P = P2 - P1 was determined by the difference between the output and input ports. The background flow velocity (vf) was varied from -20 to 20m/s, where negative values indicate flow in the opposite direction to the propagation of the acoustic wave. The flow resistance of the integrated CHR structures was calculated as Rf = \Delta P / (vf L). The absorption spectra for five selected flow velocities were computed using the “compressible potential flow” interface, in conjunction with the “linearized potential flow, frequency domain” interface.

The simulated reflection and transmission coefficients [R(\omega) and T(\omega)] were defined at the front and back surfaces of the sample, respectively. These coefficients facilitated the extraction of effective bulk modulus Keff(\omega) and density \rhoeff(\omega). The relationships are expressed as R(\omega) = S11 e^{-2ik0Lwg} and T(\omega) = S21 e^{-2ik0Lwg} [Lwg is the distance between the sample surface to the input or output port, see Supplementary Fig. 2]. For the extraction of effective properties in the experiments, the data were processed using the same algorithm as applied, except that Lwg was substituted with the distance from the sample surface to the nearest microphone.

The extracted effective properties from the CHR structures are fitted with the Lorentz model with the locked broadband duality symmetry. In addition, the dissipation factors (\beta m=d = \beta m = \beta d) are fixed according to closed-form solutions from Supplementary Note 2. The target of our fitting is to minimize the difference between the extracted \rhoeff(\omega) and Keff(\omega) and the Lorentz model, obtained via the optimization toolbox (Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm for nonlinear fitting) provided by the commercial software of MATLAB.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This is an interesting work which examines critical coupling and perfect absorption of acoustic waves in 1D two-channel scattering systems. The central idea of the work that the optimal broadband absorption conditions are realized in “duality-symmetric” resonators where the monopole- and dipole-mode coefficients (essentially, the density and compressibility) have similar resonant frequency dispersions with similar parameters. The theoretical results are supported by experimental realization of such “duality-symmetric” samples based on coupled Helmholtz resonators.
In my opinion, the results are novel, important, and, in principle, deserve publication in Nature Communications.
I have several remarks to be considered by the authors.
1. It seems to me that the duality symmetry is not the fundamental principle underlying the optimal broadband absorption but rather an artefact of the 1D two-channel scattering considered here.
Indeed, in the general 3D case, there is no duality symmetry between the scalar pressure field and vector velocity field (in contrast to the electromagnetic duality symmetry between the vector electric and magnetic fields). An acoustic analogy of the dual-symmetric approach to electromagnetism has been examined in
L. Burns et al., New J. Phys. 22, 053050 (2020).
Furthermore, the critical coupling and total absorption (zero scattering) of waves can be achieved in a single-channel non-Hermitian scattering (either reflection or transmission) without duality. See, e.g., examples in
K. Y. Bliokh et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 97, 243904 (2006); Rev. Mod. Phys. 80, 1201 (2008).
M. Asano et al., Nat. Commun. 7, 13488 (2016).
Therefore, only in the specific case of 1D acoustics (with the scalar velocity field) and two-channel scattering (requiring two conditions for the total absorption), the effective duality starts to play the key role.
2. In the general 3D case, the specific “duality” interference between the electric and magnetic dipoles (in electromagnetism) or the dipole and monopole modes (in acoustics) are well studied in the context of wave scattering by small particles.
Indeed, the duality-symmetric electromagnetic case (orthogonal electric and magnetic dipoles with appropriate phases and amplitudes) is known as the Kerker conditions, or Huygens source, which results in the vanishing backscattering. Acoustic analogues of the Kerker conditions and Huygens sources have been recently considered in
L. Wei and F. J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, New J. Phys. 22, 083016 (2020).
Y. Long et al., Natl. Sci. Rev. 7, 1024 (2020).
Moreover, the electromagnetic and acoustic Kerker effects can be generalized to the interference of higher-order multipoles.
See, e.g., recent review
I. Toftul et al., arXiv:2410.23670 (2024).
I think, in these cases, considering absorbing small particles, the duality symmetry leads to specific scattering regimes but does not provide total absorption (because of 3D geometry and multiple scattering channels).
3. Finally, the two similar resonant dependences of the density and compressibility parameters (or monopole and dipole scattering coefficient) in the problem under consideration can be considered in the context of two overlapping resonances, which can lead to “super-absorption”:
K. Ladutenko et al., Nanoscale 7, 18897 (2015).
or “super-scattering”:
Z. Ruan and S. Fan, Phys. Rev. Lett. 105, 013901 (2010).
This is probably related to Refs. [47-49] in the present paper.
Thus, I suggest the authors to consider these remarks, and discuss relations of the present work to other cases and works: 1D vs. 2D/3D cases, two-channel vs. single- and multiple-channel scatterings, duality in the context of Kerker conditions and Huygens sources, and overlapping of resonances for super-absorption.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript makes a clear and original contribution. By combining a duality transformation with causality-based absorption bounds, the authors derive a generalized two-port absorption constraint and identify broadband duality symmetry as the missing ingredient that unlocks additional absorption potential. The theoretical development is well reasoned and supported by a Lorentzian surrogate model, while the experimental implementation using CHRs demonstrates an impressively broad absorption band that convincingly outperforms a foam liner of comparable thickness. This strong agreement between theory, simulation, and experiment substantially reinforces the central claim. The authors also acknowledge current limitations (high-order modes, end corrections) and suggest possible mitigations. Overall, the work is important and well executed; however, before final acceptance in Nature Communications, I recommend minor revisions to address the following points.
(a) The step combining Eqs. (1) and (2) with AM–GM implicitly relies on the mirror/symmetric boundary mapping and the way monopole/dipole fields are superposed. Please make these symmetry/backing assumptions explicit and clarify whether Eq. (4) remains valid for asymmetric two-port boundary impedances.
(b) Eq. (7) correctly places the zeros on the real axis for single-mode Lorentzian resonators. However, in realistic multi-mode, lossy systems this condition is necessary but not sufficient. The authors should justify this and discuss the resulting limitations.
(c) The physical interpretation and impact of the higher-order correction terms δₘ(ω) and δd(ω) in the modified surrogate model remain ambiguous. Treating these higher-order contributions as frequency-independent may bias the absorption integral and the FOM at higher frequencies. The authors could provide either sensitivity curves showing how dispersive δ(ω) alters γ/Γ or a short justification beyond the 1/ω low-frequency weighting argument.
(d) The FOM depends heavily on the estimated bound Γ from simplified static calculations that neglect end corrections. As the authors note, this could underestimate Γ and thereby inflate the reported FOM values. Please quantify this possible bias.
(e)The authors neglect many recently reported high-performance, unique metamaterial absorbers (e.g., doi.org/10.1016/j.mattod.2025.06.029; Nat. Commun. 2023:14, 4028) in the state-of-the-art discussions and performance comparisons.
(f) The core advantage of ventilative design is highlighted, but no quantitative data such like pressure drop and flow resistance versus absorption performance is provided.
(g) The conclusion mentions AI/optimization but gives no concrete route to extend duality symmetry to high-order modes; can you add a brief roadmap?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript investigates the reflection and transmission properties of acoustic monopole-dipole resonators in a two-port configuration, establishing a sound absorption theory under generalized causality constraints and revealing the intrinsic connection between duality symmetry and scattering causality. The research indicates that achieving optimal absorption approaching the absorption bound not only depends on critical coupling but also requires satisfying broadband duality symmetry (equivalent to matched effective compressibility and density). Although some theoretical results have been mentioned in Ref. 23, the elaboration in this manuscript is more clear and thorough. Moreover, the designed coupled Helmholtz resonator (CHR) has experimentally observed broadband duality-symmetric sound absorption characteristics, and the further designed integrated CHR exhibits better sound absorption performance than traditional foam liners and previously reported competitive studies, with a high degree of consistency between experimental data and theoretical models. Based on this, I am willing to recommend its publication once the following issues are properly resolved.
1. The structure constructed in the manuscript is intrusive, while the foam liner used for comparison is non-intrusive, and the rigor of such a comparison is questionable. It is recommended to supplement comparative data with foam liners that have the same ventilation ratio to enhance the rigor of the research.
2. The calculation method of the experimental data in Figure 3(h) and Figure 4(e) needs to be explained. Since there is a lack of experimental data in the low-frequency region, and according to Formula 12, the integral needs to start from 0Hz, it is necessary to clarify the specific calculation process of the experimental values and the handling method for the missing low-frequency data.
3. It is necessary to clarify whether filling porous materials to change the dissipation factor β will have an impact on the volume of the air cavity that controls the modulus. In addition, listing the detailed geometric parameters of the structure in the manuscript will help readers reproduce the experimental results and conduct further verification.
4. The layout of the figures needs further optimization, such as the arrangement of images in Figure 2 and the order of subfigures in Figure 3, to improve the readability of the figures.
5. Attention should be paid to distinguishing symbols in the formulas, such as the sample thickness d and the differential symbol d, the sound pressure symbol p and the zero position p, to avoid confusion.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Causality constraints are known to bind sound absorption to a limit that can only be achieved by optimizing the system bandwidth for a specific material thickness. This limit is defined on the assumption of a one-port system, generally causing duality symmetry to be overlooked. Here, we define a generalized causality constraint of sound absorption by investigating reflection and transmission of a two-port hybrid monopole-dipole resonator. With our theory, we show that the absorption limit is approached by relying on the well-established critical coupling as well as by matching effective compressibility and density. We experimentally show that the designed resonator absorbance follows the duality symmetry condition embodied in the large bandwidth reported, confirming an intrinsic connection between duality symmetry and scattering causality. A comparison with a traditional foam liner and other competitive works further validates our findings. Our results reveal previously untapped absorption potential in broadband acoustic metamaterials.

---

## Introduction

Causality, a fundamental principle underpinning the asymmetry of unidirectional time flow, governs the upper bound of absorption integral in passive, linear, and time-invariant materials1,2. Former investigations have revealed that achieving perfect absorption at discretized frequencies requires critically coupled non-Hermitian resonances at exceptional points3,4. The manipulation of zeros and poles on the complex plane of the scattering coefficients follows the balance between the mode density and quality factors of the integrated resonator units, thus achieving broadband impedance matching and high absorption. Subsequent key developments have neared this absorption bound, demonstrated by the broadband absorption observed in multiple resonance-based metamaterials across acoustic5, elastic6 and electromagnetic domains7. Studying the absorption bound of causality constraint will guide the design wave functional devices8–11 with optimal broadband performance in the laboratory and pave the way for large-scale industrial applications12.

However, current methodologies neglect a critical question: how do fundamental symmetries dictate absorption bound throughout the entire spectrum? We find clues by considering causality constraints together with duality symmetry13, a fundamental principle embedded in numerous physics equations. For example, the supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory reveals that the strong coupling limit is remarkably equivalent to its weak coupling counterpart, with an interchange of roles between electric and magnetic charges as delineated by Montonen–Olive duality14,15. Maxwell equations are also invariant when swapping the electric and magnetic fields16. Also, duality symmetry is related to the conservation of the helicity of electromagnetic waves, attributed to the invariant degeneracy of permittivity and permeability across different geometries. In acoustics, the implications of duality symmetry are unclear for this context, due to the longitudinal wave nature, which intrinsically prohibits the helicity17. Although the analogy of acoustic duality symmetry has been proposed and investigated in the seminal work17 on the subject, the relationship between acoustic duality and scattering causality–specifically, its impact on the broadband absorption bandwidth bound of two-port systems—remains unexplored.

---

## Results

A generalized causality constraint for a two-port absorber
According to refs. 2, 5, 31 the original causality constraint for a one-port acoustic absorber is expressed as follows:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{m}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D}{c_{0} K_{eff}(0)}, (1)

where D represents the sample thickness, c0, K0 are the sound speed and bulk modulus of the background medium (e.g., air or water), and Keff(0) denotes the static effective compressibility (the inverse of the normalized bulk modulus). The variable of integration, d\omega/\omega^{2}, is proportional to d\lambda where \lambda denotes the wavelength. According to energy conservation, the absorption A(\omega) is defined as 1-|Sm(\omega)|2 where Sm(\omega) is the reflection coefficient. The derivation of Eq. (1) assumes a Neumann backing condition, which implies either \partial x p=0 or v=0, corresponding to the scattering process depicted in the left plane of Fig. 1a. Due to mirror symmetry (or anti-symmetry), this boundary condition allows for mapping the pressure field p (or velocity field v) from the left plane to the right plane. Consequently, Eq. (1) is applicable to acoustic problems involving symmetrical pressure excitation and Sm(\omega) becomes the amplitude of monopole scattering, also referred as symmetrical coherent perfect absorption32. How to reduce Keff(0) to relax the stringent constraint? This has attracted great research interests with substantial advances in recent publications9,33–35.

The 1D acoustic equations for harmonic waves can be expressed in a matrix form as: \partial x [p; v] = i\omega [0, \rho; K^{-1}, 0] [p; v], where \rho and K represent the local mass density and bulk modulus, respectively. In this context, we introduce a duality transformation that mixes the pressure and velocity fields:

[p_{\theta}; v_{\theta}] = D(\theta) [p; v] = [\cos\theta, iZ_{0}\sin\theta; i\sin\theta/Z_{0}, \cos\theta] [p; v],

where Z0 = \sqrt{\rho_{0} K_{0}} (see the detailed derivation on acoustic duality transformation with arbitrary \theta in Supplementary Note 1). If we apply a duality transformation with \theta=\pi/2, we specifically consider the exchange p \to v, \rho \to K, and \rho^{-1} \to K^{-1} between Fig. 1a, b. Consequently, the specific impedance Z=p/v is transformed into specific admittance Y=Z^{-1}=v/p. Moreover, in Eq. (1), Sm = (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0), which can be transformed into Sm \to -Sd because (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) \to -(Y-Y0)/(Y+Y0) = -(Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) = -Sm. Also, the backing condition (\partial x p=0) in Fig. 1a is also replaced by the Dirichlet one (p=0) in Fig. 1b. Therefore, the causality constraint for monopole scattering becomes the complimentary version for dipole scattering22:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{d}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D \rho_{eff}(0)}{c_{0} \rho_{0}}, (2)

where Sd(\omega) is the dipole scattering coefficient. In particular, in this case, one can afford near unity absorption over a reasonably large frequency range for a thin absorber, owing to the generally large ratio of \rho_{eff}(0)/\rho_{0}, i.e., the large imaginary part of \rho_{eff}(\omega) around the dynamic absorbing frequency leads to large static and real-valued \rho_{eff}(0), allowed by Kramer–Kronig relations.

According to the energy conservation and Eq. (3), 1-A(\omega) = |R(\omega)|2+|T(\omega)|2 = 1/2(|Sm(\omega)|2+|Sd(\omega)|2) \geq |Sm(\omega)||Sd(\omega)|. The last relation is derived from the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, or more briefly the AM–GM inequality. By converting this into the causality constraint, we have:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln(1-A(\omega)) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \ln \left| S_{m}(\omega) \right|^{2} + \ln \left| S_{d}(\omega) \right|^{2} \right) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{\pi}{c_{0} L} \left( \frac{1}{K_{eff}(0)} + \frac{\rho_{eff}(0)}{\rho_{0}} \right) = \Gamma, (4)

where L=2D (the defined thickness is effectively doubled due to mirror symmetric boundaries) and \Gamma is the established bound for the two-port setup, reflecting the static material properties. Optimal broadband absorption is defined by the proposed two-port causality constraint. Importantly, the fundamental principle lies on the fact that at long wavelength limit, all 3D scatterings of two-port problems are dominated by long wavelength scatterings as per the weighting factor (1/\omega^{2}). So, the mathematical form of causality constraint inherently embeds the role of duality for two-port 1D systems.

---

## Methods

The simulation was carried out using the COMSOL Multiphysics commercial software, specifically employing the FEM facilitated through the “pressure acoustics, frequency domain” module. The simulation setup included monitoring of incident and transmitted waves via two ports located at the boundaries of the model. The lossy components of the CHR structures, specifically the resonators’ necks and the coupling neck between cavities, were calculated by using the narrow region model. In cases where the cavities were filled with a highly absorptive porous foam69, the Johnson–Champoux–Allard model was utilized, characterized by the following parameters (also adopted from ref. 69): porosity \phi=0.94, fluid resistance Rf=32000 [Pa·s/m2], tortuosity factor \alpha=1.06, viscous characteristic length Lv=56 [\mu m], thermal characteristic length Lth=110 [\mu m]. These parameters were consistently applied across different simulations (including the foam liner in Fig. 5) to maintain a benchmark for comparison. For simulations in the time domain, the “pressure acoustics, time explicit” interface was employed.

The geometrical specifications of the single CHR are as follows (see the marked dimensions in Supplementary Fig. 2): diameter D=1.5cm, length L=2.5cm, l=0.4L, coupling channel diameter d=0.625mm, width w=1.5mm, thickness t=0.95mm, cavity height H=6.25mm, radius R=10.67mm, \tau1=3mm, \tau2=2mm. The perforated rate (or ventilation ratio) \phi=S/S0 = (\pi H^{2})/(\pi D^{2})=0.25, where S represents the cross-sectional area at the narrowest part of the main duct, and S0 denotes the wave-front area or duct cross-sectional area. The thickness of other partition walls is standardized at \Delta w=1mm. A 1/32 reduced model features a sector angle of 360/32=11.25.

The scaling of the sample in Fig. 5 adheres to the following rules: Vc \to \alpha Vc, L \to \alpha^{1/2} L, \phi \to \alpha^{-1/2} \phi, where \alpha is the scaling factor and Vc is the cavity volume occupied by porous foam. The total thickness of the integrated sample is calculated as L = (\sqrt{0.5} + \sqrt{1.5} + \sqrt{2.5} + \sqrt{4}) L0 + 3\Delta w = 14.1cm.

For the acoustic-flow interaction simulations (see Supplementary Fig. 8), the flow resistance was calculated using the “linearized Navier-Stokes, frequency domain” interface. The background pressure drop \Delta P = P2 - P1 was determined by the difference between the output and input ports. The background flow velocity (vf) was varied from -20 to 20m/s, where negative values indicate flow in the opposite direction to the propagation of the acoustic wave. The flow resistance of the integrated CHR structures was calculated as Rf = \Delta P / (vf L). The absorption spectra for five selected flow velocities were computed using the “compressible potential flow” interface, in conjunction with the “linearized potential flow, frequency domain” interface.

The simulated reflection and transmission coefficients [R(\omega) and T(\omega)] were defined at the front and back surfaces of the sample, respectively. These coefficients facilitated the extraction of effective bulk modulus Keff(\omega) and density \rhoeff(\omega). The relationships are expressed as R(\omega) = S11 e^{-2ik0Lwg} and T(\omega) = S21 e^{-2ik0Lwg} [Lwg is the distance between the sample surface to the input or output port, see Supplementary Fig. 2]. For the extraction of effective properties in the experiments, the data were processed using the same algorithm as applied, except that Lwg was substituted with the distance from the sample surface to the nearest microphone.

The extracted effective properties from the CHR structures are fitted with the Lorentz model with the locked broadband duality symmetry. In addition, the dissipation factors (\beta m=d = \beta m = \beta d) are fixed according to closed-form solutions from Supplementary Note 2. The target of our fitting is to minimize the difference between the extracted \rhoeff(\omega) and Keff(\omega) and the Lorentz model, obtained via the optimization toolbox (Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm for nonlinear fitting) provided by the commercial software of MATLAB.

### Reviewer 1

This is an interesting work which examines critical coupling and perfect absorption of acoustic waves in 1D two-channel scattering systems. The central idea of the work that the optimal broadband absorption conditions are realized in “duality-symmetric” resonators where the monopole- and dipole-mode coefficients (essentially, the density and compressibility) have similar resonant frequency dispersions with similar parameters. The theoretical results are supported by experimental realization of such “duality-symmetric” samples based on coupled Helmholtz resonators.
In my opinion, the results are novel, important, and, in principle, deserve publication in Nature Communications.
I have several remarks to be considered by the authors.
1. It seems to me that the duality symmetry is not the fundamental principle underlying the optimal broadband absorption but rather an artefact of the 1D two-channel scattering considered here.
Indeed, in the general 3D case, there is no duality symmetry between the scalar pressure field and vector velocity field (in contrast to the electromagnetic duality symmetry between the vector electric and magnetic fields). An acoustic analogy of the dual-symmetric approach to electromagnetism has been examined in
L. Burns et al., New J. Phys. 22, 053050 (2020).
Furthermore, the critical coupling and total absorption (zero scattering) of waves can be achieved in a single-channel non-Hermitian scattering (either reflection or transmission) without duality. See, e.g., examples in
K. Y. Bliokh et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 97, 243904 (2006); Rev. Mod. Phys. 80, 1201 (2008).
M. Asano et al., Nat. Commun. 7, 13488 (2016).
Therefore, only in the specific case of 1D acoustics (with the scalar velocity field) and two-channel scattering (requiring two conditions for the total absorption), the effective duality starts to play the key role.
2. In the general 3D case, the specific “duality” interference between the electric and magnetic dipoles (in electromagnetism) or the dipole and monopole modes (in acoustics) are well studied in the context of wave scattering by small particles.
Indeed, the duality-symmetric electromagnetic case (orthogonal electric and magnetic dipoles with appropriate phases and amplitudes) is known as the Kerker conditions, or Huygens source, which results in the vanishing backscattering. Acoustic analogues of the Kerker conditions and Huygens sources have been recently considered in
L. Wei and F. J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, New J. Phys. 22, 083016 (2020).
Y. Long et al., Natl. Sci. Rev. 7, 1024 (2020).
Moreover, the electromagnetic and acoustic Kerker effects can be generalized to the interference of higher-order multipoles.
See, e.g., recent review

## Paper

## Abstract

Causality constraints are known to bind sound absorption to a limit that can only be achieved by optimizing the system bandwidth for a specific material thickness. This limit is defined on the assumption of a one-port system, generally causing duality symmetry to be overlooked. Here, we define a generalized causality constraint of sound absorption by investigating reflection and transmission of a two-port hybrid monopole-dipole resonator. With our theory, we show that the absorption limit is approached by relying on the well-established critical coupling as well as by matching effective compressibility and density. We experimentally show that the designed resonator absorbance follows the duality symmetry condition embodied in the large bandwidth reported, confirming an intrinsic connection between duality symmetry and scattering causality. A comparison with a traditional foam liner and other competitive works further validates our findings. Our results reveal previously untapped absorption potential in broadband acoustic metamaterials.

---

## Introduction

Causality, a fundamental principle underpinning the asymmetry of unidirectional time flow, governs the upper bound of absorption integral in passive, linear, and time-invariant materials1,2. Former investigations have revealed that achieving perfect absorption at discretized frequencies requires critically coupled non-Hermitian resonances at exceptional points3,4. The manipulation of zeros and poles on the complex plane of the scattering coefficients follows the balance between the mode density and quality factors of the integrated resonator units, thus achieving broadband impedance matching and high absorption. Subsequent key developments have neared this absorption bound, demonstrated by the broadband absorption observed in multiple resonance-based metamaterials across acoustic5, elastic6 and electromagnetic domains7. Studying the absorption bound of causality constraint will guide the design wave functional devices8–11 with optimal broadband performance in the laboratory and pave the way for large-scale industrial applications12.

However, current methodologies neglect a critical question: how do fundamental symmetries dictate absorption bound throughout the entire spectrum? We find clues by considering causality constraints together with duality symmetry13, a fundamental principle embedded in numerous physics equations. For example, the supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory reveals that the strong coupling limit is remarkably equivalent to its weak coupling counterpart, with an interchange of roles between electric and magnetic charges as delineated by Montonen–Olive duality14,15. Maxwell equations are also invariant when swapping the electric and magnetic fields16. Also, duality symmetry is related to the conservation of the helicity of electromagnetic waves, attributed to the invariant degeneracy of permittivity and permeability across different geometries. In acoustics, the implications of duality symmetry are unclear for this context, due to the longitudinal wave nature, which intrinsically prohibits the helicity17. Although the analogy of acoustic duality symmetry has been proposed and investigated in the seminal work17 on the subject, the relationship between acoustic duality and scattering causality–specifically, its impact on the broadband absorption bandwidth bound of two-port systems—remains unexplored.

---

## Results

A generalized causality constraint for a two-port absorber
According to refs. 2, 5, 31 the original causality constraint for a one-port acoustic absorber is expressed as follows:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{m}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D}{c_{0} K_{eff}(0)}, (1)

where D represents the sample thickness, c0, K0 are the sound speed and bulk modulus of the background medium (e.g., air or water), and Keff(0) denotes the static effective compressibility (the inverse of the normalized bulk modulus). The variable of integration, d\omega/\omega^{2}, is proportional to d\lambda where \lambda denotes the wavelength. According to energy conservation, the absorption A(\omega) is defined as 1-|Sm(\omega)|2 where Sm(\omega) is the reflection coefficient. The derivation of Eq. (1) assumes a Neumann backing condition, which implies either \partial x p=0 or v=0, corresponding to the scattering process depicted in the left plane of Fig. 1a. Due to mirror symmetry (or anti-symmetry), this boundary condition allows for mapping the pressure field p (or velocity field v) from the left plane to the right plane. Consequently, Eq. (1) is applicable to acoustic problems involving symmetrical pressure excitation and Sm(\omega) becomes the amplitude of monopole scattering, also referred as symmetrical coherent perfect absorption32. How to reduce Keff(0) to relax the stringent constraint? This has attracted great research interests with substantial advances in recent publications9,33–35.

The 1D acoustic equations for harmonic waves can be expressed in a matrix form as: \partial x [p; v] = i\omega [0, \rho; K^{-1}, 0] [p; v], where \rho and K represent the local mass density and bulk modulus, respectively. In this context, we introduce a duality transformation that mixes the pressure and velocity fields:

[p_{\theta}; v_{\theta}] = D(\theta) [p; v] = [\cos\theta, iZ_{0}\sin\theta; i\sin\theta/Z_{0}, \cos\theta] [p; v],

where Z0 = \sqrt{\rho_{0} K_{0}} (see the detailed derivation on acoustic duality transformation with arbitrary \theta in Supplementary Note 1). If we apply a duality transformation with \theta=\pi/2, we specifically consider the exchange p \to v, \rho \to K, and \rho^{-1} \to K^{-1} between Fig. 1a, b. Consequently, the specific impedance Z=p/v is transformed into specific admittance Y=Z^{-1}=v/p. Moreover, in Eq. (1), Sm = (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0), which can be transformed into Sm \to -Sd because (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) \to -(Y-Y0)/(Y+Y0) = -(Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) = -Sm. Also, the backing condition (\partial x p=0) in Fig. 1a is also replaced by the Dirichlet one (p=0) in Fig. 1b. Therefore, the causality constraint for monopole scattering becomes the complimentary version for dipole scattering22:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{d}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D \rho_{eff}(0)}{c_{0} \rho_{0}}, (2)

where Sd(\omega) is the dipole scattering coefficient. In particular, in this case, one can afford near unity absorption over a reasonably large frequency range for a thin absorber, owing to the generally large ratio of \rho_{eff}(0)/\rho_{0}, i.e., the large imaginary part of \rho_{eff}(\omega) around the dynamic absorbing frequency leads to large static and real-valued \rho_{eff}(0), allowed by Kramer–Kronig relations.

According to the energy conservation and Eq. (3), 1-A(\omega) = |R(\omega)|2+|T(\omega)|2 = 1/2(|Sm(\omega)|2+|Sd(\omega)|2) \geq |Sm(\omega)||Sd(\omega)|. The last relation is derived from the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, or more briefly the AM–GM inequality. By converting this into the causality constraint, we have:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln(1-A(\omega)) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \ln \left| S_{m}(\omega) \right|^{2} + \ln \left| S_{d}(\omega) \right|^{2} \right) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{\pi}{c_{0} L} \left( \frac{1}{K_{eff}(0)} + \frac{\rho_{eff}(0)}{\rho_{0}} \right) = \Gamma, (4)

where L=2D (the defined thickness is effectively doubled due to mirror symmetric boundaries) and \Gamma is the established bound for the two-port setup, reflecting the static material properties. Optimal broadband absorption is defined by the proposed two-port causality constraint. Importantly, the fundamental principle lies on the fact that at long wavelength limit, all 3D scatterings of two-port problems are dominated by long wavelength scatterings as per the weighting factor (1/\omega^{2}). So, the mathematical form of causality constraint inherently embeds the role of duality for two-port 1D systems.

## Methods

The simulation was carried out using the COMSOL Multiphysics commercial software, specifically employing the FEM facilitated through the “pressure acoustics, frequency domain” module. The simulation setup included monitoring of incident and transmitted waves via two ports located at the boundaries of the model. The lossy components of the CHR structures, specifically the resonators’ necks and the coupling neck between cavities, were calculated by using the narrow region model. In cases where the cavities were filled with a highly absorptive porous foam69, the Johnson–Champoux–Allard model was utilized, characterized by the following parameters (also adopted from ref. 69): porosity \phi=0.94, fluid resistance Rf=32000 [Pa·s/m2], tortuosity factor \alpha=1.06, viscous characteristic length Lv=56 [\mu m], thermal characteristic length Lth=110 [\mu m]. These parameters were consistently applied across different simulations (including the foam liner in Fig. 5) to maintain a benchmark for comparison. For simulations in the time domain, the “pressure acoustics, time explicit” interface was employed.

The geometrical specifications of the single CHR are as follows (see the marked dimensions in Supplementary Fig. 2): diameter D=1.5cm, length L=2.5cm, l=0.4L, coupling channel diameter d=0.625mm, width w=1.5mm, thickness t=0.95mm, cavity height H=6.25mm, radius R=10.67mm, \tau1=3mm, \tau2=2mm. The perforated rate (or ventilation ratio) \phi=S/S0 = (\pi H^{2})/(\pi D^{2})=0.25, where S represents the cross-sectional area at the narrowest part of the main duct, and S0 denotes the wave-front area or duct cross-sectional area. The thickness of other partition walls is standardized at \Delta w=1mm. A 1/32 reduced model features a sector angle of 360/32=11.25.

The scaling of the sample in Fig. 5 adheres to the following rules: Vc \to \alpha Vc, L \to \alpha^{1/2} L, \phi \to \alpha^{-1/2} \phi, where \alpha is the scaling factor and Vc is the cavity volume occupied by porous foam. The total thickness of the integrated sample is calculated as L = (\sqrt{0.5} + \sqrt{1.5} + \sqrt{2.5} + \sqrt{4}) L0 + 3\Delta w = 14.1cm.

For the acoustic-flow interaction simulations (see Supplementary Fig. 8), the flow resistance was calculated using the “linearized Navier-Stokes, frequency domain” interface. The background pressure drop \Delta P = P2 - P1 was determined by the difference between the output and input ports. The background flow velocity (vf) was varied from -20 to 20m/s, where negative values indicate flow in the opposite direction to the propagation of the acoustic wave. The flow resistance of the integrated CHR structures was calculated as Rf = \Delta P / (vf L). The absorption spectra for five selected flow velocities were computed using the “compressible potential flow” interface, in conjunction with the “linearized potential flow, frequency domain” interface.

The simulated reflection and transmission coefficients [R(\omega) and T(\omega)] were defined at the front and back surfaces of the sample, respectively. These coefficients facilitated the extraction of effective bulk modulus Keff(\omega) and density \rhoeff(\omega). The relationships are expressed as R(\omega) = S11 e^{-2ik0Lwg} and T(\omega) = S21 e^{-2ik0Lwg} [Lwg is the distance between the sample surface to the input or output port, see Supplementary Fig. 2]. For the extraction of effective properties in the experiments, the data were processed using the same algorithm as applied, except that Lwg was substituted with the distance from the sample surface to the nearest microphone.

The extracted effective properties from the CHR structures are fitted with the Lorentz model with the locked broadband duality symmetry. In addition, the dissipation factors (\beta m=d = \beta m = \beta d) are fixed according to closed-form solutions from Supplementary Note 2. The target of our fitting is to minimize the difference between the extracted \rhoeff(\omega) and Keff(\omega) and the Lorentz model, obtained via the optimization toolbox (Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm for nonlinear fitting) provided by the commercial software of MATLAB.

## Paper

## Abstract

Causality constraints are known to bind sound absorption to a limit that can only be achieved by optimizing the system bandwidth for a specific material thickness. This limit is defined on the assumption of a one-port system, generally causing duality symmetry to be overlooked. Here, we define a generalized causality constraint of sound absorption by investigating reflection and transmission of a two-port hybrid monopole-dipole resonator. With our theory, we show that the absorption limit is approached by relying on the well-established critical coupling as well as by matching effective compressibility and density. We experimentally show that the designed resonator absorbance follows the duality symmetry condition embodied in the large bandwidth reported, confirming an intrinsic connection between duality symmetry and scattering causality. A comparison with a traditional foam liner and other competitive works further validates our findings. Our results reveal previously untapped absorption potential in broadband acoustic metamaterials.

---

## Introduction

Causality, a fundamental principle underpinning the asymmetry of unidirectional time flow, governs the upper bound of absorption integral in passive, linear, and time-invariant materials1,2. Former investigations have revealed that achieving perfect absorption at discretized frequencies requires critically coupled non-Hermitian resonances at exceptional points3,4. The manipulation of zeros and poles on the complex plane of the scattering coefficients follows the balance between the mode density and quality factors of the integrated resonator units, thus achieving broadband impedance matching and high absorption. Subsequent key developments have neared this absorption bound, demonstrated by the broadband absorption observed in multiple resonance-based metamaterials across acoustic5, elastic6 and electromagnetic domains7. Studying the absorption bound of causality constraint will guide the design wave functional devices8–11 with optimal broadband performance in the laboratory and pave the way for large-scale industrial applications12.

However, current methodologies neglect a critical question: how do fundamental symmetries dictate absorption bound throughout the entire spectrum? We find clues by considering causality constraints together with duality symmetry13, a fundamental principle embedded in numerous physics equations. For example, the supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory reveals that the strong coupling limit is remarkably equivalent to its weak coupling counterpart, with an interchange of roles between electric and magnetic charges as delineated by Montonen–Olive duality14,15. Maxwell equations are also invariant when swapping the electric and magnetic fields16. Also, duality symmetry is related to the conservation of the helicity of electromagnetic waves, attributed to the invariant degeneracy of permittivity and permeability across different geometries. In acoustics, the implications of duality symmetry are unclear for this context, due to the longitudinal wave nature, which intrinsically prohibits the helicity17. Although the analogy of acoustic duality symmetry has been proposed and investigated in the seminal work17 on the subject, the relationship between acoustic duality and scattering causality–specifically, its impact on the broadband absorption bandwidth bound of two-port systems—remains unexplored.

---

## Results

A generalized causality constraint for a two-port absorber
According to refs. 2, 5, 31 the original causality constraint for a one-port acoustic absorber is expressed as follows:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{m}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D}{c_{0} K_{eff}(0)}, (1)

where D represents the sample thickness, c0, K0 are the sound speed and bulk modulus of the background medium (e.g., air or water), and Keff(0) denotes the static effective compressibility (the inverse of the normalized bulk modulus). The variable of integration, d\omega/\omega^{2}, is proportional to d\lambda where \lambda denotes the wavelength. According to energy conservation, the absorption A(\omega) is defined as 1-|Sm(\omega)|2 where Sm(\omega) is the reflection coefficient. The derivation of Eq. (1) assumes a Neumann backing condition, which implies either \partial x p=0 or v=0, corresponding to the scattering process depicted in the left plane of Fig. 1a. Due to mirror symmetry (or anti-symmetry), this boundary condition allows for mapping the pressure field p (or velocity field v) from the left plane to the right plane. Consequently, Eq. (1) is applicable to acoustic problems involving symmetrical pressure excitation and Sm(\omega) becomes the amplitude of monopole scattering, also referred as symmetrical coherent perfect absorption32. How to reduce Keff(0) to relax the stringent constraint? This has attracted great research interests with substantial advances in recent publications9,33–35.

The 1D acoustic equations for harmonic waves can be expressed in a matrix form as: \partial x [p; v] = i\omega [0, \rho; K^{-1}, 0] [p; v], where \rho and K represent the local mass density and bulk modulus, respectively. In this context, we introduce a duality transformation that mixes the pressure and velocity fields:

[p_{\theta}; v_{\theta}] = D(\theta) [p; v] = [\cos\theta, iZ_{0}\sin\theta; i\sin\theta/Z_{0}, \cos\theta] [p; v],

where Z0 = \sqrt{\rho_{0} K_{0}} (see the detailed derivation on acoustic duality transformation with arbitrary \theta in Supplementary Note 1). If we apply a duality transformation with \theta=\pi/2, we specifically consider the exchange p \to v, \rho \to K, and \rho^{-1} \to K^{-1} between Fig. 1a, b. Consequently, the specific impedance Z=p/v is transformed into specific admittance Y=Z^{-1}=v/p. Moreover, in Eq. (1), Sm = (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0), which can be transformed into Sm \to -Sd because (Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) \to -(Y-Y0)/(Y+Y0) = -(Z-Z0)/(Z+Z0) = -Sm. Also, the backing condition (\partial x p=0) in Fig. 1a is also replaced by the Dirichlet one (p=0) in Fig. 1b. Therefore, the causality constraint for monopole scattering becomes the complimentary version for dipole scattering22:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln \left| \frac{1}{S_{d}(\omega)} \right|^{2} \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{2\pi D \rho_{eff}(0)}{c_{0} \rho_{0}}, (2)

where Sd(\omega) is the dipole scattering coefficient. In particular, in this case, one can afford near unity absorption over a reasonably large frequency range for a thin absorber, owing to the generally large ratio of \rho_{eff}(0)/\rho_{0}, i.e., the large imaginary part of \rho_{eff}(\omega) around the dynamic absorbing frequency leads to large static and real-valued \rho_{eff}(0), allowed by Kramer–Kronig relations.

According to the energy conservation and Eq. (3), 1-A(\omega) = |R(\omega)|2+|T(\omega)|2 = 1/2(|Sm(\omega)|2+|Sd(\omega)|2) \geq |Sm(\omega)||Sd(\omega)|. The last relation is derived from the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means, or more briefly the AM–GM inequality. By converting this into the causality constraint, we have:

\int_{0}^{\infty} \ln(1-A(\omega)) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \ln \left| S_{m}(\omega) \right|^{2} + \ln \left| S_{d}(\omega) \right|^{2} \right) \frac{d\omega}{\omega^{2}} \leq \frac{\pi}{c_{0} L} \left( \frac{1}{K_{eff}(0)} + \frac{\rho_{eff}(0)}{\rho_{0}} \right) = \Gamma, (4)

where L=2D (the defined thickness is effectively doubled due to mirror symmetric boundaries) and \Gamma is the established bound for the two-port setup, reflecting the static material properties. Optimal broadband absorption is defined by the proposed two-port causality constraint. Importantly, the fundamental principle lies on the fact that at long wavelength limit, all 3D scatterings of two-port problems are dominated by long wavelength scatterings as per the weighting factor (1/\omega^{2}). So, the mathematical form of causality constraint inherently embeds the role of duality for two-port 1D systems.

---

## Methods

The simulation was carried out using the COMSOL Multiphysics commercial software, specifically employing the FEM facilitated through the “pressure acoustics, frequency domain” module. The simulation setup included monitoring of incident and transmitted waves via two ports located at the boundaries of the model. The lossy components of the CHR structures, specifically the resonators’ necks and the coupling neck between cavities, were calculated by using the narrow region model. In cases where the cavities were filled with a highly absorptive porous foam69, the Johnson–Champoux–Allard model was utilized, characterized by the following parameters (also adopted from ref. 69): porosity \phi=0.94, fluid resistance Rf=32000 [Pa·s/m2], tortuosity factor \alpha=1.06, viscous characteristic length Lv=56 [\mu m], thermal characteristic length Lth=110 [\mu m]. These parameters were consistently applied across different simulations (including the foam liner in Fig. 5) to maintain a benchmark for comparison. For simulations in the time domain, the “pressure acoustics, time explicit” interface was employed.
